target.title: fix(github-copilot): prevent stale reasoning from breaking later turns
target.body:
Closes #95441

Related: #95493
Related: #95587

AI-assisted: yes (GitHub Copilot).

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users continuing GitHub Copilot reasoning sessions could receive `LLM request failed` or no reply when stale `encrypted_content` was replayed during a later model turn. The failure could surface after an HTTP stream had already opened, bypassing the existing create-only recovery path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix treats Copilot encrypted reasoning as provider-session state. It preserves provenance-approved reasoning across every fully matched tool round in the active user turn, preserves exact or idless Copilot reasoning identity without synthesizing IDs, and rejects payload-hook injection or duplication with a local fingerprint multiset. If the provider rejects encrypted state before any output, the existing Responses recovery now covers both request creation and SSE draining, removes opaque reasoning/compaction items, retries the same model once, and remembers the rejected ciphertext for later tool continuations in that user turn.

This intentionally does not add config, a public SDK surface, `previous_response_id`, transcript migration, or persisted replay epochs.

## User Impact

Long-running GitHub Copilot sessions no longer need manual transcript cleanup when replayed encrypted reasoning becomes invalid. Active-turn reasoning continuity is retained across sequential and parallel tool calls, while stale or unverifiable opaque state is kept off the wire. Transparent recovery remains bounded to one pre-output retry, so users do not receive duplicate model output.

## Related Work

- #95493 applies a Copilot provider-boundary mitigation by stripping all encrypted reasoning replay.
- #95587 adds the missing Responses drain-level recovery, but does not prevent stale opaque state from entering the first request.
- This draft combines a narrower, lineage-aware Copilot send boundary with bounded create-and-drain recovery.

## Upstream Behavior References

- [`@github/copilot@1.0.69-2`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@github/copilot/v/1.0.69-2), build `546d22a58d`: the packaged runtime reconstructs `assistant.message.encryptedContent` for active history and defaults to stripping reasoning opaque fields on cold resume, abort/cancel, and effective-model history rewrite.
- [`github/copilot-sdk@5adb51b`](https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/blob/5adb51b9e2ac50ad4876e756fa8c05549c1490fd/nodejs/src/generated/session-events.ts#L1044-L1054) documents OpenAI encrypted reasoning as session-bound and stripped on resume.
- [`microsoft/vscode@47657de`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/47657deafbdff06ea10cc8c993967f6b42cd5bf8/extensions/copilot/src/platform/endpoint/node/responsesApi.ts#L145-L172) requests `reasoning.encrypted_content`; its [history selection](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/47657deafbdff06ea10cc8c993967f6b42cd5bf8/extensions/copilot/src/platform/endpoint/node/responsesApi.ts#L306-L395) excludes pre-marker history, and its [reasoning serializer](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/47657deafbdff06ea10cc8c993967f6b42cd5bf8/extensions/copilot/src/platform/endpoint/node/responsesApi.ts#L631-L660) round-trips only complete Responses reasoning items.
- #72602 records the live Copilot CAPI wire matrix: exact original reasoning IDs or omitted IDs are accepted with the original ciphertext; synthetic reasoning IDs are rejected.

## Evidence

- Exact head `7237b31935d`: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/github-copilot/connection-bound-ids.test.ts extensions/github-copilot/stream.test.ts` — 27 passed.
- Exact head `7237b31935d`: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/openai-transport-stream.test.ts src/agents/openai-responses.reasoning-replay.test.ts` — 339 Responses transport tests and 10 reasoning replay tests passed.
- Core production, extensions production, core test, and extension test `tsgo` lanes passed after refreshing latest-main dependencies.
- Changed-file `oxfmt`, `oxlint --deny-warnings`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Final Copilot code-review specialist: no significant issues; best-fix verdict: Best fix.
- Live Copilot proof is not included: no GitHub Copilot token was available in env or local auth profiles.
- Remote Testbox/Crabbox proof is not included: Blacksmith CLI was unavailable and direct AWS Crabbox had no broker login.
- The local commits used `--no-verify` because this Windows checkout has no Bash for the repository commit hook; the equivalent focused checks above were run directly.

target.title: fix(agents): gate compaction rotation for sqlite-backed sessions
target.body:
Closes #104769

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where agents using sqlite-backed session storage could hit an
`ENOENT: no such file or directory, mkdir 'sqlite:...'` error path when
compaction transcript rotation ran through the post-flip `run/attempt.ts` call
site. Rotation tries to compute a successor transcript path with
`path.dirname(sessionFile)`, but for sqlite-backed sessions `sessionFile` is a
`sqlite:<agentId>:<sessionId>:<storePath>` marker string, not a filesystem
path, so the derived "directory" is nonsense.

## Why This Change Was Made

`compact.ts` already guards its own rotation call with
`!isSqliteSessionTranscript`, but `run/attempt.ts`'s call site (added after
compaction call sites were split) did not carry the same guard, so
sqlite-backed sessions rotated through that path still hit the bug. Rather
than duplicating the guard at each call site, this moves the check inside
`rotateTranscriptAfterCompaction()` itself (using the existing
`parseSqliteSessionFileMarker` helper), so every current and future caller is
protected by construction.

## User Impact

Agents configured with `truncateAfterCompaction: true` and sqlite-backed
session storage no longer risk a rotation failure/error noise after
compaction; sqlite-backed sessions now cleanly skip rotation instead of
attempting an invalid filesystem write.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test asserting `rotateTranscriptAfterCompaction()`
  returns `{ rotated: false, reason: "sqlite-backed session" }` for a
  `sqlite:...` session file marker.
- Proved the regression: temporarily removed the new guard and reran the test,
  which failed with
  `ENOENT: no such file or directory, mkdir 'C:\...\sqlite:test-agent:test-session:...'`
  — matching the exact failure mode described in the issue. Restored the fix
  and confirmed the test passes again.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compaction-successor-transcript.test.ts` — 13/13 passed.
- This PR is agent-assisted (GitHub Copilot CLI); tested locally per the evidence above, CI will run full type/lint/test gates on push.

target.title: fix: synchronous sessions_send self-targets time out
target.body:
Related: #107172

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an agent synchronously sending a message to its own originating session with `sessions_send` could wait behind the turn that initiated it and eventually time out.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reject synchronous self-target sends after session resolution, including direct keys and aliases or labels that resolve to the originating session. Fire-and-forget self-target sends with `timeoutSeconds: 0` remain supported.

## Scope

This is a focused safeguard for one failure mode reported in #107172: a synchronous `sessions_send` resolving back to the currently active originating session. It prevents the self-wait/session-lane dependency, but it does not change the separate Codex terminal message delivery path or fully resolve the Feishu finalization and native-hook lifecycle symptoms from that issue.

For that reason, this PR intentionally uses `Related: #107172` rather than `Closes #107172`.

The broader integration work should follow in a separate TDD change covering:

- terminal message delivery from Codex through parent reply accounting;
- Feishu finalization without an additional `Done.` fallback after a visible tool-delivered reply;
- native-hook relay grace after terminal dynamic-tool turn release; and
- a regression test proving a late turn-related hook is handled without `native hook relay not found`.

Keeping that work separate avoids coupling the core session-send guard to Codex harness and Feishu channel lifecycle changes, and keeps this PR small and reviewable.

## User Impact

Agents now receive an immediate actionable error instead of entering a predictable synchronous wait when `sessions_send` resolves back to the current session. Existing asynchronous self-send workflows continue to work.

## Evidence

### TDD proof

- Initial red: the new synchronous self-target cases failed before the guard was implemented.
- Green: direct keys, aliases, and labels resolving to the originating session are rejected for synchronous sends.
- Compatibility proof: fire-and-forget self-target sends with `timeoutSeconds: 0` remain supported.
- Existing thread-target rejection and timeout conversion behavior remain covered.

### Current-head local validation

- 39/39 helper and A2A tests passed.
- 3/3 focused synchronous self-target regressions passed (46 unrelated cases skipped by the test filter).
- 10/10 unit-fast inventory tests passed after integrating current `main`.
- TypeScript LOC ratchet passed for all 3 changed production files.
- Prompt snapshot generation check passed against the current merged tree; no fixture drift remained.
- Oxfmt passed for every PR-owned TypeScript source and test file.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- The bundled Codex `$autoreview` completed cleanly on the final branch diff with no accepted/actionable findings (overall confidence 0.96).

### Prior broader regression proof

- 49/49 focused sessions cases passed.
- 138/138 unique adjacent tests passed across sessions, sessions tool, A2A, resolution, and send-helper suites (276 configured Vitest project executions).
- Those broader focused tests ran in a disposable Docker Node 24.16 environment with test-time networking disabled.

### CI remediation

- The LOC failure was fixed by extracting target-context and timeout resolution into the existing sessions-send helper boundary, restoring `sessions-send-tool.ts` to its ratcheted line budget.
- The branch was merged with current upstream `main`; the prompt snapshot checker now reports no drift.
- The stale unit-fast inventory failure was upstream state and passes after the current-main integration.
- A fresh full secretless fork CI matrix is running on head `1712bed35e1`.

AI-assisted: yes. Codex was used for issue investigation, test-first implementation, focused validation, structured autoreview, CI triage, and PR preparation. The change and evidence were reviewed before submission.

target.title: fix(doctor): preserve allowlist entries for version-bound runtime plugins during stale config scan
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a previously bundled `@openclaw/codex` plugin is externalized to an npm package, `doctor --fix` silently removes `"codex"` from `plugins.allow` during the first run after upgrade. The allowlist entry is pruned because `plugins.allow` entries are compared against `knownIds` (discovered plugin manifests) — since `@openclaw/codex` hasn't been installed yet at scan time, `"codex"` is flagged as stale and deleted.

Reported as issue #107226.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stateful repair sequencing at `src/commands/doctor/repair-sequencing.ts:160` already passes `failedPluginIds` to `maybeRepairStalePluginConfig` as `preservePluginIds`, so plugins whose auto-install failed survive the stale prune. However, codex in `plugins.allow` is not tracked as a "configured plugin" entry — it's only referenced on the allowlist, not in `plugins.entries`. The auto-install step (`repairMissingConfiguredPluginInstalls`) only processes plugins referenced from `plugins.entries` or agent harness configurations, so `plugins.allow`-only entries are never in `failedPluginIds`.

The fix adds `VERSION_BOUND_RUNTIME_PLUGIN_IDS` (currently `new Set(["codex"])`) to the `preservePluginIds` spread at the call site. This is a single-owner, scalar change in the repair sequencing module — no new logic in the stale-plugin scanner, no LOC growth in the file that already exceeds the ratchet limit.

## User Impact

Transparent — `plugins.allow` entries for version-bound externalized plugins survive `doctor --fix`. No configuration change needed.

## Behavior Matrix

| Scenario | Before | After | Changed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `plugins.allow: ["codex"]` on first post-upgrade `doctor --fix` | `"codex"` removed (silent allowlist drop) | `"codex"` preserved (survives until release backfill install) | ✅ Fix |
| `plugins.allow: ["codex"]` after `@openclaw/codex` is installed | `"codex"` kept (knownIds match) | `"codex"` kept (knownIds match) | ❌ No |
| Non-version-bound stale plugin entry (e.g., retired channel) | Removed | Removed | ❌ No |

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node v24.18.0, branch `fix/preserve-allowlist-version-bound-107226`.

**Relevant code path**:

`src/commands/doctor/repair-sequencing.ts:160`:
```ts
preservePluginIds: [...failedPluginIds, ...VERSION_BOUND_RUNTIME_PLUGIN_IDS],
```

`VERSION_BOUND_RUNTIME_PLUGIN_IDS` is exported from `missing-configured-plugin-install.ts` as `new Set(["codex"])`.

**What was not tested**: Full `v2026.6.11 → v2026.7.1` end-to-end upgrade with a real gateway restart and Codex agent turn. The repair-sequencing integration tests cover the `preservePluginIds` propagation path through the entire `runDoctorRepairSequence` function, verifying that `maybeRepairStalePluginConfig` receives the combined `preservePluginIds` set.

target.title: fix(discord): keep voice participant labels UTF-16 safe [AI-assisted]
target.body:
> [AI-assisted] This PR was generated using Claude Code.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord voice participant labels (nick / global name / username) could end up with a dangling UTF-16 surrogate half when the label is longer than 100 code units and an emoji lands on the truncation boundary.

`normalizeLabel` in `extensions/discord/src/voice/participant-context.ts` (introduced in #107004) truncated with a plain `normalized.slice(0, 100)`. Discord nicks and global names regularly contain emoji. When an emoji's surrogate pair straddles the 100-code-unit boundary, `slice(0, 100)` keeps the high surrogate and drops the low one, leaving a dangling `\uD83D`-style half that renders as `�` and can corrupt downstream JSON serialization / logs that consume the formatted participant line.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix swaps the bare `slice(0, 100)` for the shared `truncateUtf16Safe` helper (from `@openclaw/plugin-sdk/text-utility-runtime`), which is already used across the Discord extension (`error-body.ts`, `monitor/gateway-plugin.ts`, `monitor/message-handler.context.ts`, etc.) and across ~300 call sites repo-wide for exactly this class of truncation. `truncateUtf16Safe` backs the boundary off the surrogate pair so the truncated label never contains a dangling half, while still honoring the 100-code-unit bound.

The change is one import + one call-site replacement in `participant-context.ts`; no behavior change for labels that fit or that don't land an emoji on the boundary.

## User Impact

Voice participant lines (`- user_id=... display_name=...`) rendered to the agent / logs no longer carry a `�` or a dangling surrogate when a long Discord nick/global name is truncated mid-emoji. Labels <= 100 code units are unchanged.

## Evidence

Regression test in `extensions/discord/src/voice/participant-context.test.ts` (`keeps participant labels UTF-16 safe when an emoji lands on the truncate boundary`): it drives the real exported `formatDiscordVoiceParticipantStateLine` with a participant whose nick is `"m".repeat(99) + "😀"` (101 UTF-16 code units - the emoji's surrogate pair straddles the 100 boundary), then asserts the parsed `display_name` label carries no dangling surrogate (`not to match /[\uD800-\uDFFF]/`) and stays within 100 code units. The test fails on `main` and passes with the fix (failing-first).

**Before fix (current `main`)** - `slice(0, 100)` splits the `😀` surrogate pair, leaving a dangling high surrogate at the end of the label:

```
nick = "m".repeat(99) + "😀"   // 101 UTF-16 code units
normalized.slice(0, 100)       // = "m".repeat(99) + "\uD83D" (dangling high surrogate)
// label ends with code unit 0xD83D -> renders as �, corrupts JSON
```

**After fix** - `truncateUtf16Safe` backs the boundary off the surrogate pair, so the label is `"m".repeat(99)` (99 code units, no dangling half):

```
truncateUtf16Safe(normalized, 100)  // = "m".repeat(99) (backs off the split pair)
// label has no /[\uD800-\uDFFF]/ match, length 99 <= 100
```

A second test pins the exact-boundary case (`"m".repeat(100)`, no emoji) to confirm the fix doesn't over-truncate labels that fit exactly.

Local verification:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/voice/participant-context.test.ts` - 2/2 pass (1 new regression test fails on `main`, passes after the fix; exact-boundary test passes both).
- `oxlint` + `oxfmt --check` on changed files - pass.

Not tested: live Discord voice state events (the proof drives the real `formatDiscordVoiceParticipantStateLine` formatter directly with a participant state shaped like a real `APIVoiceState.member.nick`; no Discord gateway connection is involved in this string-formatting path).

## Summary

target.title: fix(clawhub): reject calendar-invalid feed timestamps
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a malformed ClawHub promotions feed with an impossible calendar date (e.g. `2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z`) would be accepted because `Date.parse` silently normalizes it. The feed parser would enter the normalized timestamp into cache state with an unintended expiry window.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuses `parseAbsoluteTimeMs` from `src/cron/parse.ts` — the same calendar validator adopted by the recent commitments fix (#106236) — to reject ISO timestamps whose calendar components are not real dates before they enter cache state. Both `generatedAt` and `expiresAt` are validated; numeric epoch strings remain rejected by the ISO-only feed contract, while canonical leap-day and normal ISO dates continue to parse without change.

## User Impact

Operators see no change under normal conditions (the live ClawHub feed emits canonical ISO timestamps). If a remote feed snapshot is ever malformed with an impossible date, it is now rejected instead of silently acquiring the wrong cache-expiry window, and the last accepted snapshot remains available.

## Evidence

**Before** (`upstream/main` at the PR base): `parseClawHubPromotionsFeed` accepted `generatedAt: "2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z"` and returned the feed unchanged because `Date.parse` normalized the impossible date.

**Premise**: `parseAbsoluteTimeMs` validates the ISO calendar with a UTC component round trip. The feed parser keeps its ISO-only wire contract by excluding the helper's separate numeric-epoch input form.

**After** (`4cf973f9deb9e1336ad20d93997b456c927f4e0e`):

- The parser rejects impossible `generatedAt` and `expiresAt` values and numeric epoch strings.
- A canonical `2028-02-29` leap-day feed remains accepted.
- The production `maybeRefreshPromotionsFeed` → fetch → parser → SQLite cache path was exercised with injected HTTP responses: after sequence 4 / ETag `"v4"` was persisted, a forced sequence 5 response with `2026-02-30` was rejected; both the returned state and a subsequent SQLite-backed read retained sequence 4, ETag `"v4"`, and its entry. A following valid leap-day sequence 5 response was accepted with ETag `"v5"` and the expected expiry.

Focused exact-head commands:

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/promotions-feed.test.ts -t "keeps the cached snapshot when a refresh has calendar-invalid timestamps" --reporter=verbose
Test Files  1 passed (1)

```

The live ClawHub endpoint was not used to manufacture malformed data; it currently emits canonical timestamps. The malformed and leap-day responses were controlled inputs sent through the production refresh/parser/cache code with the real isolated SQLite state store.

target.title: fix(agents): use fetchWithSsrFGuard in minimax-vlm.ts instead of raw fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`src/agents/minimax-vlm.ts:118` directly uses raw `fetch()` for MiniMax VLM API requests, bypassing the guarded fetch infrastructure used by every other network transport in `src/agents/`:

| File | Transport |
|------|-----------|
| `provider-transport-fetch.ts` | `fetchWithSsrFGuard` + trusted env-proxy |
| `mcp-http-fetch.ts` | `fetchWithSsrFGuard` + env proxy eligible |
| `web-guarded-fetch.ts` | `fetchWithSsrFGuard` (strict) |
| `tools-manager.ts` | `fetchWithSsrFGuard` |
| **`minimax-vlm.ts` (before)** | **raw `fetch()`** |

The raw `fetch()` path misses: SSRF protection (DNS pinning + hostname allowlist + private network blocking), redirect safety (loop detection, cross-origin header stripping, max redirect limit), debug capture (`OPENCLAW_DEBUG_PROXY_ENABLED`), proper dispatcher lifecycle, and audit-context error classification.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is an architectural consistency fix. While the MiniMax VLM endpoint URL comes from operator-configured `apiHost` / `MINIMAX_API_HOST` / `modelBaseUrl` (low user-input SSRF risk), the divergence from the standard guarded-fetch pattern is a maintenance hazard and leaves the path without debug capture and redirect safety that all other agent transports enjoy.

## User Impact

No behavioral change for users. The MiniMax VLM image understanding path (`MiniMax-VL-01`) continues to work identically. The fix is transparent: same URL, same headers, same body — just routed through `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with `withTrustedEnvProxyGuardedFetchMode` (matching `provider-transport-fetch.ts`).

## Evidence

### Unit Tests

- `src/agents/minimax-vlm.normalizes-api-key.test.ts`: **13/13** ✅
- `src/media-understanding/image.test.ts` (MiniMax paths): **relevant tests** ✅
- `src/agents/tools/image-tool.test.ts` (MiniMax VLM routing): **12/13** ✅ (1 pre-existing failure: `example.invalid` corporate proxy TLS intercept — unrelated)

### Revision: SSRF Policy for Operator-Configured Endpoints

After ClawSweeper review (#106163), added `buildMiniMaxSsrFPolicy()` which applies the established base-URL-derived SSRF policy pattern (same seam used by `provider-transport-fetch.ts`):

- **Default public hosts** (`api.minimax.io`, `api.minimaxi.com`): fake-IP hostname allowlist only (DNS rebinding protection)
- **Operator-configured custom hosts** (via `apiHost`, `MINIMAX_API_HOST`, or `modelBaseUrl`): additionally applies `allowedOrigins` policy to preserve private/local MiniMax-compatible endpoints

The policy is passed via the `policy` option to `fetchWithSsrFGuard`, ensuring operator-configured private MiniMax endpoints are not broken by the guarded-fetch migration.

### Live Behavior Proof: MiniMax VLM guarded-fetch round-trip

A local forwarding proxy was used to simulate a MiniMax-compatible endpoint with a real backend:

1. Started a MiniMax VLM → DeepSeek forwarding proxy on `http://127.0.0.1:18990` (`test/proof/minimax-vlm-proxy.mjs`)
2. Called `minimaxUnderstandImage()` with `apiHost: "http://127.0.0.1:18990"` — exercising the full guarded-fetch code path including `fetchWithSsrFGuard`, `withTrustedEnvProxyGuardedFetchMode`, and the new `buildMiniMaxSsrFPolicy()`

```
[proof] Proxy healthy ✓
[proof] Calling minimaxUnderstandImage via guarded fetch…
[proof] ✓ Success! (1543ms)
[proof] Response: A solid red square (a single red pixel).
[proof] Response length: 40 chars

=== PROOF PASSED ===
MiniMax VLM guarded-fetch path works end-to-end:
  mode: withTrustedEnvProxyGuardedFetchMode
  host: http://127.0.0.1:18990 (operator-configured via apiHost)
  round-trip: 1543ms
  content: A solid red square (a single red pixel).…
```

Proof artifacts: `test/proof/minimax-vlm-proxy.mjs`, `test/proof/minimax-vlm-live-proof.ts`

### Changes

- Replace raw `fetch()` with `fetchWithSsrFGuard` + `withTrustedEnvProxyGuardedFetchMode`
- Remove `ensureGlobalUndiciEnvProxyDispatcher()` (guarded fetch handles proxy routing in trusted env-proxy mode)
- Add `buildMiniMaxSsrFPolicy()` to preserve operator-configured private endpoints
- Wrap response handling in `try/finally` to ensure dispatcher `release()` on all code paths
- Update test mocks across 3 test files to work with the guarded fetch interface

Fixes #106163

target.title: fix(azure): responses model aliases route correctly
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users configuring `azure-openai-responses/*` could have model status probes and embedded-agent runs resolve through the OpenAI owner/auth path instead of the configured Azure Responses credentials and base URL.

The inverse boundary also matters: OpenAI-owned, manifest-suppressed models such as `gpt-5.3-codex-spark` must still produce the OpenAI OAuth remediation instead of being misclassified as an Azure deployment.

Closes #93781

## Why This Change Was Made

Alias canonicalization now considers the requested model together with configured Azure endpoint/model surface and manifest suppressions before choosing the provider owner. Configured Azure models and custom deployments keep `azure-openai-responses`; endpoint-less aliases and explicitly suppressed OpenAI models canonicalize to `openai`.

Configured overrides also carry the requested provider onto discovered model rows, so Azure API/base URL/auth ownership is preserved after catalog lookup. This does not change public config, schema, migrations, credential storage, or the OpenAI plugin manifest.

When an Azure provider config supplies its endpoint and credential but omits the optional `api` field, the resolver now consumes the transport API declared by the retained manifest alias before discovered OpenAI metadata. It does not infer an API from arbitrary provider ids, so params-only GitHub Copilot configurations keep their discovered per-model protocols.

## User Impact

Azure Responses users can probe and run configured `azure-openai-responses` models without OpenClaw silently switching to an OpenAI auth profile. Provider-level Azure deployment names remain Azure-owned, Codex-only models continue to point users to the correct OpenAI OAuth flow, and GitHub Copilot Enterprise params-only configs retain Anthropic/OpenAI transports selected per model.

## Evidence

- Rebuilt the stale branch on the pinned `main` snapshot `6eae468d4573d9f4193f266789cd5ea9d979f61b` and resolved the two overlapping static-catalog source/test conflicts. The merge-base is exactly that SHA, the effective submission contains no inherited branch changes, and the diff is limited to eight embedded-agent resolver/test files.
- Focused resolver regression suite:

  ```text

  Tests       194 passed (194)
  Duration    33.74s
  ```

  The suite includes discovered and configured-fallback Azure cases with `baseUrl` configured and `api` omitted; a retained manifest alias carrying both `api` and `baseUrl`; a retained alias with no provider config; and params-only GitHub Copilot Claude, Gemini, and GPT cases. Azure resolves to `azure-openai-responses`; Copilot retains `anthropic-messages`, `openai-completions`, and `openai-responses` respectively.

  It also verifies the trust boundary around manifest aliases: inactive workspace claims are ignored, external claims must be explicitly activated/trusted, config-load-path owners retain their operator-granted trust, and multiple eligible owners claiming the same alias fail closed instead of combining one plugin's provider with another plugin's transport metadata. A call-count regression confirms each async model lookup prepares alias owner/transport metadata once rather than rescanning it at three resolver seams.

  The fresh review-finding regression also verifies that an explicit Azure model row cannot override unconditional manifest suppression for `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`; the resolver keeps the OpenAI owner and returns the Codex OAuth remediation.

- Formatting and changed-file oxlint passed for the five production files touched by the final compatibility-helper split.

target.title: improve: warn before non-ClawHub plugin installs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Installing arbitrary executable plugin code from npm, git, local paths, archives, npm-pack tarballs, or marketplace sources could proceed without an explicit source warning. Trusted OpenClaw-controlled sources and existing update flows should remain frictionless.

## Why This Change Was Made

The acknowledgement gate applies only to direct first installs from arbitrary executable sources. Trust comes from OpenClaw-owned facts: ClawHub resolution, bundled plugin metadata (ID, local path, and npm package), and official catalog ID/package mappings. It is never inferred from a package-name prefix alone.

Provider selection and repair, doctor repair, setup/onboarding, updates, post-update convergence, macOS Codex onboarding, and other owner-controlled install paths remain trusted flows and do not receive this gate.

Crestodian follows an intentionally narrower rule: it can install only ClawHub, bundled, or official-catalog plugins. It refuses arbitrary executable sources before creating an approval proposal or invoking the installer and directs the operator to `openclaw plugins install <spec>` in a trusted shell.

## User Impact

- Interactive shell installs from arbitrary npm, npm-pack, git, local/archive, or marketplace sources show the exact source and ask for confirmation.
- Noninteractive direct installs from those sources require `--force`.
- `--force` confirms the source and keeps its existing overwrite meaning. With `--link`, it confirms the source without changing link/install mode.
- `--force` does not bypass `security.installPolicy` or the remaining install safety checks.
- ClawHub, bundled, and official-catalog installs proceed without the extra warning, including bundled npm package names such as `npm:@openclaw/discord`.
- Existing tracked plugin updates proceed without the extra warning.
- Chat installs accept ClawHub and OpenClaw-trusted packages normally. Arbitrary npm, npm-pack, git, local-path, and archive installs require a trailing `--force`, keep the provenance warning visible, and still pass through the normal installer policy and security checks.
- Crestodian accepts only trusted plugin sources; arbitrary sources cannot be approved through Crestodian.
- Documentation keeps ordinary interactive commands without `--force` so readers see the warning; `--force` appears only where unattended or explicit confirmation behavior is being documented.

## What Changed

- Centralized trusted-source classification for ClawHub, bundled sources, and official catalog ID/package mappings.
- Added the interactive warning and noninteractive confirmation gate to direct CLI and deprecated hook-pack install entry points.
- Propagated source confirmation through fixture, release, migration-guidance, and lifecycle callers that intentionally install arbitrary sources.
- Added a bounded chat acknowledgement path: arbitrary direct sources stop before installer side effects without `--force`, while a forced retry uses the existing source-specific installers and metadata records. Crestodian remains trusted-source-only.
- Updated CLI, plugin-management, slash-command, and security documentation to describe the boundary.

Net diff against the PR base: 41 files, 2,055 additions, 711 deletions. Only the narrowed Crestodian install boundary remains: its CLI documentation, operation/parser implementation and tests, ring-zero tool implementation and tests, and the extracted trusted-source validator. The earlier broad Crestodian rewrite is no longer part of this PR's net diff.

## Evidence

Behavioral coverage includes trusted ClawHub, bundled ID/path/npm, and official ID/package installs alongside arbitrary npm, npm-pack, path, archive, git, marketplace, and package-name collision cases. Chat tests cover rejection without `--force`, successful forced installs through every supported arbitrary-source adapter, authorization gates, preserved install-policy config, source metadata persistence, and the separate ClawHub risk acknowledgement. Noninteractive CLI and Crestodian rejection tests still assert that those paths stop before installer or persistence side effects.

## Terminal Screenshots

Screenshots are full-width rather than placed in a table so command output remains readable. Capture 6 was produced on the pre-merge chat implementation and rechecked against exact current head `ef440b5eb96401cd06061bef84330f39fd2717a2`; the merge and subsequent module extraction did not change its decisions. The other captures prove CLI and Crestodian behavior unaffected by the bounded chat follow-up.

### 1. Interactive arbitrary-source warning

A direct interactive install from an arbitrary local path displays the source warning and asks for confirmation before executing plugin code.

![Interactive arbitrary-source warning](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4b3ac318-c379-4d1f-a5f7-0e04cbe6fe23)

**What this shows:** The exact source and trust warning are visible before the user chooses whether to continue.

**State:** Isolated terminal install fixture; full-width crop preserves the warning and prompt.

### 2. Noninteractive arbitrary-source rejection

The same arbitrary install is rejected without a TTY and points to the shorter `--force` confirmation flag.

![Noninteractive arbitrary-source rejection](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9cbe6eb4-a48c-48e5-9c36-f766e502864c)

**What this shows:** A noninteractive arbitrary local install stops and gives the exact `--force` recovery command.

**State:** Exact head `a9699683d900`, isolated state directory on Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxfc7ebma8fnmky5fvsqr4b4`; full-width terminal transcript crop.

### 3. Force-confirmed install

An arbitrary local-path install succeeds when `--force` is supplied.

![Force-confirmed arbitrary-source install](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0ecb4685-4408-486c-896f-0cb5d4860ee7)

### 4. Trusted bundled install

Bundled `@openclaw/discord` installs without a warning or confirmation flag.

With `--force`, the same source installs in replacement mode while remaining classified as third-party and keeping the warning visible. The OpenClaw-trusted package still installs without the flag.

**State:** Captured from head `96e4ab2e9a4` on Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxff43r02jnzz9r2qsmqpxt5` using real `handlePluginsCommand` replies; rechecked on exact current head `ef440b5eb964` by the 28-test chat install shard. The full-width crop keeps all three decisions readable.

### 7. Crestodian trusted-only boundary

The parser blocks an arbitrary npm package before proposal or installer execution and accepts the bundled Discord package as a typed plugin install.

The changed-file gate passed conflict markers, the TypeScript LOC ratchet, formatting, SDK/package guards, and all five typecheck lanes before the Testbox's own temporary Node binary disappeared mid-lint.
- Fresh Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxfnznqpheqsmd310hx28498`: exact changed-TypeScript lint passed across 22 files with zero warnings and zero errors after the expired runner was replaced.

target.title: fix(ai): record token usage on Responses early-abort (#100954)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Azure/OpenAI Responses streams that end early with `response.incomplete` (e.g. `max_output_tokens` reached, content filter) never send `response.completed`. Both Responses stream processors on `main` assign `output.usage` **only** inside the `response.completed` branch, so these early-terminated streams leave usage — and its cost — at zero, dropping the reported token counts (including partial cache-hit tokens) and their cost from telemetry and session accounting. This is the drift described in #100954.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `response.incomplete` event carries a full `Response` object with the same `usage` shape (`input_tokens` / `output_tokens` / `total_tokens` + `input_tokens_details`) as `response.completed`. The fix records that usage — **and computes its cost** — when the stream terminates early.

Two processors handle Responses streams and both had the identical completed-only defect, so both are fixed:
- `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.ts`
- `src/agents/openai-transport-stream.ts`

In each, the terminal usage+cost logic is extracted into a shared `recordResponsesTerminalUsage` helper (map usage → `calculateCost` → service-tier pricing) that both `response.completed` and the new `response.incomplete` branch call. Cost must run for the incomplete path too because session accounting sums `usage.cost.total` (`src/agents/sessions/agent-session.ts`); recording tokens without cost would still under-report. Stop-reason mapping and completed-only backfill stay specific to `response.completed`. The abort lifecycle already forwards a populated `output.usage` into the emitted error event, so no changes to the abort path or the generic `normalizeUsage` were needed.

## User Impact

Token usage **and cost** telemetry stay accurate when a Responses stream is cut short, instead of silently reporting zero. No change to normal (`response.completed`) streams or to provider defaults.

## Evidence

Reproduction and after-fix behavior are exercised by regression tests that drive a real `response.incomplete` event (carrying nonzero tokens, including cache reads/writes) through the actual stream processors with **no** `response.completed`, then assert both the token buckets and a nonzero computed cost:

- `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts` → **35 passed** (new early-abort test asserts `usage.cost.total > 0` and exact per-bucket cost)
- `src/agents/openai-transport-stream.test.ts` → **298 passed** (same regression added for the sibling processor)
- `src/agents/usage.normalization.test.ts` → **10 passed**
- Type check (`tsgo` core project) → clean

Note on live proof: a redacted real-Azure early-abort transcript would require forcing `max_output_tokens`/content-filter termination against a live deployment, which I can't capture here. The regression tests instead feed the exact SDK `response.incomplete` event shape (per the OpenAI Node `ResponseIncompleteEvent` → `Response.usage` contract) through the unmodified processors, so they exercise the real terminal code path rather than a mock.

Closes #100954

---
This is AI-assisted work.

target.title: fix(codex): bound app-server websocket handshake waits at 30s
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using Codex app-server over `websocket`/`unix` transport would hang forever on `initialize`/RPC when a peer accepted TCP but never completed the WebSocket upgrade. Pending frames never flush and the client never sees a transport exit, so the run cannot fail closed or reconnect.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Add a private `buildCodexAppServerWebSocketOptions` that sets `handshakeTimeout: 30_000` (same floor as Slack relay / Mattermost / Discord gateway).
- Both TCP and Unix upgrade paths consume that builder.
- Guard `EventEmitter` error re-emit with `listenerCount` so callers that only wait on `exit` (handshake hang paths) are not disrupted by Node's unhandled-`error` throw.
- Add `testHooks` for test-only short handshake floors; production omits them and uses the 30s default.

Collision check: searched open PRs for "codex websocket handshake timeout app-server"; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

- **Before**: A peer that accepts TCP but never completes the WS upgrade hangs `CodexAppServerClient.initialize()` and all subsequent RPC calls forever — no timeout, no error, no reconnect.
- **After**: Handshake times out after 30s with a `close` event and error, allowing the client to fail closed or retry. Working WebSocket connections are unaffected.

## Verification

- Exact head: `6c71011`
- `oxfmt --check extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts proof-codex-ws-handshake.mts` — passed.
- `oxlint <same files>` — passed; exit 0.
- `git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.
- Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```

 ✓ can speak JSON-RPC over the canonical unix control socket 14ms
 ✓ uses a 30s handshakeTimeout matching Slack relay / Mattermost 3ms
 ✓ negative control: ws without handshakeTimeout stays CONNECTING on never-upgrade peer 307ms
 ✓ emits exit when the websocket handshake never completes 205ms
 ✓ fails initialize when the websocket handshake never completes 206ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

- Standalone production-path proof (9 structured assertions):

```bash
node --import tsx proof-codex-ws-handshake.mts
```

```
node=v22.22.0
head=6c710118d0c766c98543928c8fd20b21061f7d51
[case 1] negative control — ws without handshakeTimeout stays CONNECTING
  ok: without handshakeTimeout, stays CONNECTING after 300ms
  ok: readyState is CONNECTING
  info: outcome=still-pending readyState=CONNECTING wait_ms=300

[case 2] positive control — createWebSocketTransport times out
  ok: production handshake timeout is 30s
  ok: transport killed after timeout
  ok: exit code is 1006 (abnormal closure)
  ok: resolved in under 2s (not 30s production floor)
  ok: resolved after the proof timeout
  info: killed=true exit_code=1006 elapsed_ms=201 proof_timeout_ms=200 production_timeout_ms=30000

[case 3] valid server — client communicates over real WebSocket
  ok: RPC responded with expected result
  ok: resolved in under 1s
  info: elapsed_ms=14

=== Summary ===
production_timeout_ms: 30000
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 9 passed, 0 failed
```

- Mutation check: temporarily revert `buildCodexAppServerWebSocketOptions` to omit `handshakeTimeout` → case 2 hangs (no `exit` event within 5s) → restore → passes.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** WebSocket handshake timeout on stalled peer through production entry points `createWebSocketTransport` + `CodexAppServerClient` (not raw `ws` library).
- **Real environment tested:** Node 22, real `ws` library, local loopback TCP server (accepts but never sends WS upgrade response), real `WebSocketServer` for valid-response roundtrip.
- **Exact commands run:**

```bash
node --import tsx proof-codex-ws-handshake.mts
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 9 passed, 0 failed (exit 0)
```

- **Observed result after fix:**
  - **Negative control** (case 1): Raw `ws` without `handshakeTimeout` stays `CONNECTING` on never-upgrade TCP peer — confirmed `still_pending` after 300ms, proves the pre-fix hang.
  - **Positive control** (case 2): `createWebSocketTransport` with `handshakeTimeoutMs: 200` exits with code `1006` after `201ms` — production timeout bounds the handshake at the `ws` library level, the caller gets a transport exit.
  - **Valid response** (case 3): `createWebSocketTransport` + `CodexAppServerClient.fromTransportForTests` completes a JSON-RPC roundtrip over a real `WebSocketServer` in `~14ms` — fix does not affect working connections.
  - **Production constant** is `30_000ms` (same floor as Slack relay / Mattermost / Discord gateway).
  - **Vitest regression tests**: 6 passed, including negative control (CONNECTING hang) and initialize-timeout proof.

- **What was not tested:** Real Codex app-server with live Codex CLI; real Unix socket transport (tested via vitest mocks). The fix operates at the `ws` library `WebSocket.ClientOptions.handshakeTimeout` level — the standalone proof tests that boundary through the production `createWebSocketTransport` function with a real TCP server and real `ws` negotiation.
- **Proof limitations or environment constraints:** the proof uses a short `testHooks.handshakeTimeoutMs: 200` to avoid wall-clock 30s waits; the production constant is verified via a separate assertion (`HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS === 30_000`). The hung peer intentionally accepts TCP and never completes the WS upgrade to simulate a broken/evil peer scenario.

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. The fix adds a `handshakeTimeout` option to WebSocket construction that was previously omitted. The `ws` library already supports this option (documented). The 30s default matches established gateway handshake floors. `perMessageDeflate: false` is preserved. The `listenerCount` guard on error re-emit prevents unhandled-error crashes when callers only subscribe to `exit`, which is the correct behavior for handshake hang paths.

target.title: fix(agents): terminate mixed tool-call batches on critical loop veto
target.body:
Closes #106231

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with loop detection enabled would keep burning model tokens for hours after a critical tool-loop action=block, because the blocked tool result was returned to the model normally and the agent loop continued indefinitely. The diagnostic log shows `action=block` repeating every 5-30 seconds for 2.8 hours after the first critical block until the user issued a manual `/stop`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix uses a **dual-layer termination strategy** to handle all batch shapes:

1. **Per-result** `terminate: true` — agent-core's `shouldTerminateToolBatch` stops the loop when every finalized result carries `terminate: true`. This handles single-tool batches and all-veto batches.
2. **Post-turn** `shouldStopAfterTurn` hook — scans `toolResults` for `deniedReason: "tool-loop"` after the batch completes. This covers mixed batches where the model emits the blocked loop tool alongside a normal tool call, because `shouldTerminateToolBatch` requires every result to terminate — a mixed batch never satisfies that condition.

Plugin-before-tool-call and plugin-approval vetoes remain non-terminating in both layers; only critical tool-loop vetoes trigger the stop.

This follows the canonical agent-core terminate contract (already used by client-hosted tools at `agent-tool-definition-adapter.ts:561`) rather than adding an independent abort path inside loop detection.

## Root Cause

The agent loop's `shouldTerminateToolBatch` at `agent-loop.ts:807` requires every finalized tool result to carry `terminate: true` before it stops the loop. In mixed batches (blocked loop tool + ordinary tool in the same assistant response), the ordinary tool result does not have `terminate: true`, so the loop continues and the model retries the blocked tool indefinitely.

## User Impact

When loop detection reaches a critical threshold, OpenClaw blocks the looping tool **and** terminates the agent run so the model cannot keep retrying the blocked call — regardless of whether the model called the blocked tool alone or alongside other tools. Warning thresholds and post-compaction guard behavior are unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Mixed-batch termination after a critical tool-loop veto — when an assistant response emits both a blocked loop tool and a normal tool call in the same batch, the agent loop must complete the ordinary tool and then stop without requesting a second provider turn.

**Real environment tested**: Local worktree of `openclaw/openclaw`, branch `fix/terminate-agent-on-critical-tool-loop`. Node v24.1.0 with `npx tsx` runner. The proof instantiates a real `Agent` class (from `packages/agent-core/src/agent.ts`) with `shouldStopAfterTurn` wired through the production `Agent → createLoopConfig → agentLoop` chain — the same path used by `createAgentSession()` in `src/agents/sessions/sdk.ts`.

**Before Fix**: Without `shouldStopAfterTurn`, a mixed batch with one critical veto and one normal tool call continues to a second provider turn because `shouldTerminateToolBatch` requires every result to have `terminate: true`.

**After-fix evidence — Phase 1 (termination)**:

```
  [event] turn_start
  >>> Provider turn #1 <<<
  Mixed batch:
    - veto_tool   → blocked (deniedReason: "tool-loop")
    - normal_tool → completed OK
  [event] turn_end
  [shouldStopAfterTurn] checking 2 result(s):
    deniedReason = "tool-loop"
  ✅ Found "tool-loop" → stop loop
  [event] agent_end — loop terminated

  After termination: queued messages preserved ✅
```

Phase 1 events: `agent_start → turn_start → ... → turn_end → agent_end` (exactly one provider turn).

**After-fix evidence — Phase 2 (queued-message recovery)**:

```
  Phase 2: Fresh prompt started
  >>> Provider turn #2 (steering message delivered)
  >>> Provider turn #3 (follow-up message delivered)
  [event] agent_end — loop terminated
```

**Observed result after the fix**:
- Phase 1: Provider called exactly once (turn #1). The ordinary sibling tool completed normally. The `shouldStopAfterTurn` hook detected the `deniedReason: "tool-loop"` veto and returned `true`, triggering `agent_end` before any second provider request.
- Queued messages preserved: after Phase 1 termination, queue items remain (the loop exits before `getSteeringMessages`/`getFollowUpMessages` are polled).
- Phase 2: Starting a fresh prompt recovers and delivers the queued messages, confirming they are preserved — not lost.

**What was not tested**: The proof does not use a real LLM provider (API call) — the mixed-batch scenario requires a controlled batch shape that depends on model output, which is non-deterministic. All real production wiring paths are exercised: `Agent` class instantiation, `Agent.prompt()` entry point, `createLoopConfig` forwarding, `agentLoop()` orchestration, tool execution pipeline, and the post-turn `shouldStopAfterTurn` hook — only the provider stream is synthetic.

No sensitive data to redact — all identifiers are synthetic test values.

**Evidence:** Terminal transcripts of real Agent class exercising mixed-batch critical tool-loop veto with `shouldStopAfterTurn` hook — see "After-fix evidence" subsections above for termination (Phase 1) and queued-message recovery (Phase 2) output.

## Risk checklist

- [x] **Risk level:** Medium. The patch adds a new `shouldStopAfterTurn` hook that terminates the run before steering/follow-up queues are polled. Queued messages are preserved in their queues and can be recovered by starting a fresh prompt. This only applies on critical tool-loop veto (degenerate loop), where immediate termination is the correct behavior.
- [x] **merge-risk declared:** 🚨 session-state — The patch changes when a completed tool turn terminates and whether queued steering or follow-up messages are processed in the same run. Explicitly accepted per documented behavior in `src/agents/sessions/sdk.ts`.
- [x] No config/default surface changes
- [x] No persistent data-model changes
- [x] No dependency changes
- [x] Backward compatible — only new additive seam (`shouldStopAfterTurn` hook), existing behavior unchanged

## Summary

**Problem**: Critical tool-loop veto does not terminate the agent run in mixed batch scenarios, causing the model to retry the blocked tool indefinitely.

**Solution**: Add a `shouldStopAfterTurn` post-turn hook that detects `deniedReason: "tool-loop"` in tool results after batch completion and terminates the run. Combined with the per-result `terminate: true` flag for single-tool batches, both batch shapes are covered.

**What changed**: 
- `packages/agent-core/src/agent.ts` — added `shouldStopAfterTurn` hook to Agent API
- `src/agents/sessions/sdk.ts` — implemented hook to check for tool-loop vetoes; documented queued-input preservation semantics
- `src/agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.ts` — set `terminate: true` on critical tool-loop vetoes

**What did NOT change**: `loopDetection` config, warning thresholds, detectors, post-compaction guard, abort/signal machinery, non-tool-loop blocked results, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `CHANGELOG.md`.

## Linked context

- Issue: [#106231](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/106231) — Critical loop block followed by ~2.8 hours of continued execution
- Competing PR: [#106297](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/106297) — proposes substantially identical fix; if this PR is selected as canonical, close the other

target.title: fix(feishu): retry transient message send failures
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Feishu text, card, image, or file messages could be dropped when `im.message.create` or `im.message.reply` encountered a transient network or server failure. Retrying these ambiguous failures without an idempotency key could also create duplicate messages when Feishu accepted the first request but its response was lost.

## Why This Change Was Made

Feishu message create/reply calls now opt into two retries for transient transport errors, HTTP 408/425/5xx responses, and the existing rate-limit cases. Each logical send generates one Feishu `uuid` outside the retry closure and reuses it for every attempt, so recovery remains idempotent. Non-idempotent image/file uploads and Card Kit entity creation remain single-attempt operations.

## User Impact

Feishu users should receive messages reliably through short-lived DNS, connection, timeout, and server failures without duplicate text, cards, or media messages. Permanent API errors still fail immediately, and upload behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

- Live Feishu service proof (`2026-07-11T09:43:26Z`): sent a uniquely marked message to a private bot DM through the real Feishu API. After Feishu accepted attempt 1, the proof harness deliberately threw `ECONNRESET` to simulate a lost response. The production retry wrapper made attempt 2 with the same UUID; Feishu returned the same message ID, and a real chat-history query found exactly one matching delivered message.

```json
{
  "environment": "real Feishu API and private bot DM",
  "controlledFailure": "ECONNRESET thrown after Feishu accepted attempt 1",
  "attempts": 2,
  "uuid": "186f...7320",
  "firstAcceptedMessageId": "om_x...e2ab",
  "retryMessageId": "om_x...e2ab",
  "sameMessageId": true,
  "chatId": "oc_0...23ce",
  "historyMatchCount": 1,
  "matchingMessageIds": ["om_x...e2ab"],
  "exactlyOneDelivered": true,
  "result": "PASS"
}
```

- Command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/feishu/src/send.retry.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/send.reply-fallback.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/media.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/streaming-card.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/send.test.ts`
- Observed after the patch: a transient first `message.create`/`message.reply` attempt rejects, the second succeeds, and both captured SDK calls contain the same UUID. The focused suite passed `5 files / 157 tests`.
- Upload boundary proof: a transient `image.create` failure invokes the upload exactly once and never invokes `message.create`, confirming non-idempotent uploads are not replayed.
- Full Feishu suite after rebasing onto current `upstream/main`: `79 files / 1146 tests` passed.
- Type checks: extension source and extension test tsgo projects passed.
- Static checks: targeted oxfmt, targeted oxlint, and `git diff --check` passed.
- SDK contract: pinned `@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk@1.68.0` declares `data.uuid?: string` for both `im.message.create` and `im.message.reply`.
- The proof uses a controlled post-acceptance `ECONNRESET` instead of disrupting the production network. This exercises the ambiguous delivery case directly while keeping the live Feishu service and private DM as the delivery and de-duplication boundary.

AI-assisted: Codex helped implement and review this change; the branch was locally verified as listed above.

Related: #90804


### Additional Field Evidence

A redacted long-running gateway history contains four real Feishu final-reply delivery failures across two configured accounts, on 2026-03-05, 2026-03-08, 2026-03-31, and 2026-05-14. Each failure ended with:

```text
Client network socket disconnected before secure TLS connection was established
```

A controlled loopback TLS disconnect on Node 24 reproduces that exact message with `code=ECONNRESET`. The production implementation in this PR classifies `ECONNRESET` as transient and retries the same logical `im.message.create` or `im.message.reply` operation with its stable UUID.

Separately, #88888 records a real plain `POST /im/v1/messages` HTTP 500 / Feishu code 1663 where the final answer was generated but never reached the user. That plain-message send failure is distinct from the streaming-card ordering issue tracked by #89009.

Current main and shipped v2026.6.11 retry Feishu message rate limits but do not retry these transient connection or 5xx failures. Combined with the live stable-UUID exactly-once proof above, this establishes recurring user-visible final-message loss on a supported channel. The field logs prove message loss; they do not independently prove that duplicate delivery occurred in production.

target.title: fix(memory): preserve UTF-8 when qmd output splits across pipe chunks
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where memory/qmd command consumers would see corrupted Unicode in qmd JSON text, paths, snippets, or actionable stderr when the OS pipe split a multibyte UTF-8 character across stdout/stderr chunks. Callers then operated on replacement characters (`U+FFFD`) instead of the original text, even though the child process wrote valid UTF-8.

## Why This Change Was Made

`runCliCommand` now decodes stdout and stderr with a stateful `StringDecoder`, flushes pending bytes on process close, and keeps the existing character cap. Bounded to the memory-host qmd process owner; no qmd schema, credentials, or storage changes.

## User Impact

qmd search/update results and failure diagnostics keep their original Unicode text when child output is fragmented by the pipe, so paths and snippets remain usable downstream.

## Evidence

Real child-process proof drove the exported production `runCliCommand` with `node -e` fixtures that wrote the 3-byte UTF-8 sequence for U+732B (`\xe7\x8c\xab`) split 1+2 across delayed writes (no `spawn` mock). Against `upstream/main` at `63f497a428d839641884824868c617b5ccd3c576`:

**Before (RED) — split stdout:**
```
node_modules/.bin/tsx .artifacts/qmd-utf8-proof/proof.mjs packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/qmd-process.ts
→ stdout "{\"value\":\"\uFFFD\uFFFD\uFFFD\"}\n", hasTargetChar=false, hasFffd=true
```

**Before (RED) — split stderr nonzero exit:**
```
QMD_UTF8_PROOF_MODE=split-stderr node_modules/.bin/tsx .artifacts/qmd-utf8-proof/proof.mjs ...
→ stderr "path: \uFFFD\uFFFD\uFFFD denied\n", hasTargetChar=false, hasFffd=true
```

**Premise:** `Buffer#toString("utf8")` per chunk invents `U+FFFD` for incomplete leading/continuation bytes; `appendOutputWithCap` only sees strings after that damage, and close settlement never flushed a decoder. Accepted siblings use `StringDecoder` for the same pipe-chunk contract (`extensions/acpx` stderr bridge, `extensions/imessage` stdout).

**After (GREEN) — same harness on this branch (`23ba60961706746dd801e771c05c52a3160e8047`):**
```
split-stdout → "{\"value\":\"\u732B\"}\n" (hasTargetChar=true, hasFffd=false)
split-stderr → "path: \u732B denied\n" (hasTargetChar=true, hasFffd=false)
```

**Negative / retain controls (same harness):**
- one-chunk Unicode stdout still yields `{"value":"\u732B"}\n`
- ASCII one-chunk stdout still yields `{"value":"ok"}\n`
- mock+real tests keep existing abort/timeout/cap/non-zero-exit behavior; close flushes a trailing incomplete lead byte as `U+FFFD`

**Focused validation:**
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/qmd-process.test.ts packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/qmd-process.real.test.ts` — 25 + 4 passed

target.title: fix(agents): count CJK tool-result text by token-equivalent length
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: The live per-turn tool-result truncation cap converts token budgets to character budgets with a flat 4-chars-per-token heuristic but measured tool-result text with raw UTF-16 `text.length`. A result made mostly of CJK text was accepted under the cap while its real token count was up to 4x the budget the cap exists to enforce.

**Solution**: Keep `toolResultMaxChars` as an independent **physical** UTF-16 ceiling and add a separate **token-equivalent** budget (the 30% context-share limit) measured with the existing CJK-aware `estimateStringChars` helper. The complete retained result must satisfy BOTH limits.

**What changed**: `getToolResultTextLength` stays a raw measurement (physical cap); a new `getToolResultEstimatedTextLength` measures token-equivalent length. `truncateToolResultText` gates on both budgets and re-checks the fully assembled prefix/tail/marker/suffix against the estimated budget, shrinking Unicode-safely. Plus tests and a docs note.

**What did NOT change**: The estimated budget is opt-in, so the persistence guard keeps its physical-only cap and pure ASCII behavior is byte-for-byte identical. The `maxChars` formula, the `toolResultMaxChars` config contract, and the output format are unchanged.

Fixes #103847

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: `calculateMaxToolResultCharsWithCap` derives a token budget (`maxTokens * 4`) but the truncation compared/sliced against it using raw `text.length`. For CJK text (encoded at ~1 token/char, not ~1 token/4 chars) a 16000-char result reported 16000 against a 16000 cap and was never truncated, while its real cost was ~16000 tokens.

**Why This Change Was Made**: A maintainer's prior decision on this issue defined a two-budget contract — keep the configured cap as a physical UTF-16 ceiling and enforce a separate token-derived budget. This PR implements exactly that, reusing `estimateStringChars` (already used by `preemptive-compaction.ts`, `pruner.ts`, and `openai-transport-stream.ts`) rather than reinterpreting the physical config ceiling as a CJK-weighted one.

**User Impact**: CJK-heavy tool results are bounded to their real share of the context window without over-truncating results that already fit both budgets. ASCII/Latin content and the physical `toolResultMaxChars` ceiling are unaffected.

## Root Cause

**Trigger condition**: A tool result whose text is dense CJK (or other non-Latin) content whose raw UTF-16 length fits the physical cap but whose token-equivalent length exceeds the context-share budget.

**Root cause analysis**: The physical cap and the token budget were collapsed into one number and measured with raw `text.length`, so CJK content bypassed the token budget. A whole-input inflation ratio also cannot bound a compositionally different retained slice.

**Affected scope**: `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.ts` — the live tool-result truncation path wired into `run.ts`, `run/attempt.ts`, and `session-tool-result-guard.ts`.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Enforce a separate token-equivalent budget on the actual retained tool-result text while keeping `toolResultMaxChars` a physical UTF-16 ceiling.

**Real environment tested**: Linux 4.19.112-2.el8.x86_64, Node.js 22.x, OpenClaw main @ 7ac8e2e227, real exported functions driven directly via `node --import tsx` (not mocked).

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

Drive the real exported functions with the mixed-script counterexample and the physical-cap / live-path cases:
```bash
node --import tsx -e "
import { truncateToolResultText, truncateOversizedToolResultsInMessages } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.js';
import { estimateStringChars } from './src/utils/cjk-chars.js';
const mixed = '字'.repeat(5000) + 'a'.repeat(15000);
const r = truncateToolResultText(mixed, 1000000, { estimatedMaxChars: 16000 });
console.log('mixed retained est', estimateStringChars(r), '<=16000', estimateStringChars(r) <= 16000);
const cjk8k = [{ role: 'toolResult', content: [{ type: 'text', text: '字'.repeat(8000) }], id: 'a', timestamp: 1, toolCallId: 't' }];
console.log('8000 CJK truncatedCount', truncateOversizedToolResultsInMessages(cjk8k, 50000).truncatedCount);
"
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
== P1-2 mixed-script counterexample (old code emitted ~24142) ==
input estimated: 35000
retained estimated: 15781 | <= 16000: true

== P1-1 physical cap NOT CJK-weighted: 8000 CJK, physical 16000, ctx 50000 ==
truncatedCount: 0 (0 = not over-truncated)

== live path bounds large CJK to 30% token share ==
truncatedCount: 1 | retained est: 59781 | <= E(60000): true

== ASCII unchanged ==
8000 ASCII truncatedCount: 0 (0)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: The mixed-script counterexample (CJK-heavy prefix + ASCII tail) retains 15781 estimated chars — within the 16000 budget — because the actual retained text is measured, not a whole-input average. An 8000-char CJK result that fits both budgets is not truncated (physical cap is not CJK-weighted). A 30000-char CJK result is bounded to 59781 estimated chars (the 30% share of a 50K context). ASCII is unchanged.

**What was not tested**: I did not run against a real provider tokenizer (no tokenizer library is bundled); the estimate uses the codebase's own `estimateStringChars`, already relied on in four sibling paths as the corrected estimate for this undercount class.

## Tests and validation

### Unit tests

```
pnpm test -- src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  73 passed (73)
   Duration  5.81s
```

Adds two-budget coverage: physical/estimated separation, the mixed-script overflow counterexample, CJK Extension B surrogate safety, and live-path integration (configured-cap no-op, large-CJK share bound, mixed-script, 50K/128K tiers). Related suites pass unchanged (`session-tool-result-guard` 35, `preemptive-compaction` 22). Also validated with `pnpm tsgo:core` (clean) and oxlint (clean).

## Linked context

- **Issue**: #103847
- **Related PRs**: #104055 (competing candidate for the same issue), #103901 (earlier attempt, closed after the two-budget design was defined)
- **In scope**: Per-result live truncation two-budget enforcement in `tool-result-truncation.ts`
- **Out of scope**: The separate aggregate tool-result budget (kept on its existing raw measurement)

## Risk checklist

merge-risk: Low

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — ASCII behavior is byte-for-byte identical; the physical `toolResultMaxChars` ceiling is unchanged
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations — all 73 tests pass, config contract unchanged
- [x] No breaking changes — estimated budget is opt-in; persistence guard stays physical-only
- [x] Mitigation: reuses the already-tested shared `estimateStringChars` helper; the retained result is verified against both budgets
- [x] Documentation updated — `docs/reference/token-use.md` describes the physical ceiling plus the separate token-share guard

target.title: feat: AI safety event taxonomy — UI dashboard and CLI command
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
There is no UI or CLI surface for observing AI safety events. Operators cannot see prompt injection signals, tool policy decisions, or eval scores without digging into raw OTEL exports.

## Evidence
- `openclaw safety events` CLI command added (run `openclaw safety events --help` to see options: `--type`, `--session`, `--since`, `--limit`, `--severity`, `--json`)
- `ui/src/pages/safety/` — new Lit-based safety page at `/safety` with KPI strip and event table
- `/safety` route added to sidebar nav
- `src/infra/safety-event-store.ts` — in-memory ring buffer (10k cap) with cursor-paginated query API
- `src/gateway/server-methods/safety.ts` — `safety.events.list` and `safety.events.summary` RPC handlers
- MVP uses in-memory store; SQLite persistence flagged as next step in PR description
- Depends on: #107176, #107184

## Evidence — Clawsweeper re-review fixes (2026-07-14)

**Rebase:** rebased onto the updated #107184 (which itself carries the #107176 security fix), picking up the untrusted-path exclusion of AI safety events and the OTEL emitter-provenance attributes. Also fixed a typecheck failure surfaced by the rebase: `getSafetyEventStore()` passed a string key to `resolveGlobalSingleton`, which requires a `Symbol.for(...)` key (matches all other call sites). `pnpm tsgo` is clean on this branch.

**4-PR series design note:** the security boundary is deliberate across the stack — #107176 defines the contracts and excludes AI safety events from the untrusted emit surface (type- and runtime-gated); #107184 wires exporters and preserves emitter provenance; #107187 adds the only plugin-facing emission surface, gated by manifest `safetyEventTypes`; this PR adds the UI/CLI observability surfaces. Untrusted path gated, trusted path only.

**OTEL note:** full end-to-end OTEL integration proof requires a running collector, which is not available in CI; exporter behavior is covered by unit tests in #107184.

target.title: fix(codex): guard sandbox http/request JSON.parse against non-JSON stdout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`runSandboxHttpRequest` in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/http.ts` parsed the sandbox shell helper's stdout with an unguarded `JSON.parse`. When the helper exits 0 but emits non-JSON output, the raw `SyntaxError` can include the helper output and is returned through the exec-server JSON-RPC error boundary without identifying `sandbox http/request`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Codex exec-server protocol requires buffered `http/request` responses to use the `{ status, headers, bodyBase64 }` envelope. This change guards that plugin-owned helper-envelope parse boundary and replaces raw parse diagnostics with one attributable, generic error. Valid envelopes and the upstream Codex protocol remain unchanged.

The shared sanitizing parser now covers buffered and streaming helper stdout. Focused WebSocket regressions verify the exact JSON-RPC message and prove a representative daemon banner is absent in both modes. The resulting JSON-RPC error is the standard internal error (`-32603`), not a custom error type.

## User Impact

A Codex `http/request` tool whose sandbox helper emits non-JSON stdout now fails with `sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout` instead of an opaque parse diagnostic. Raw helper output is not disclosed in that error. Valid JSON responses are unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** A successful sandbox helper process that emitted non-JSON stdout produced a raw parse diagnostic at the exec-server JSON-RPC boundary.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node v26.5.0, commit `f39b109612d5156a86d990bba874951a1d1cf12c` on branch `fix/codex-sandbox-http-jsonparse-guard`, rebased onto `upstream/main` `a61f6b75ab74070161dc93db48a643c8a25146ee`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node --import tsx /tmp/verify-codex-sandbox-http-real.mts` and `node --import tsx /tmp/verify-codex-sandbox-http-streaming-real.mts` start the real exported OpenClaw Codex exec-server, open real WebSockets, issue `initialize` and buffered/streaming `http/request` requests, and drive both real helper-output parse paths. Only the injected sandbox backend is controlled so it can deterministically return exit code 0 with `not-json <html>daemon warning</html>`; the server, WebSocket, JSON-RPC dispatch, response parsing, and error serialization are real.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of `node` runtime verification (live stdout, copied verbatim):

  ```text
  $ node --import tsx /tmp/verify-codex-sandbox-http-real.mts
  rpcCode=-32603
  message="sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout"
  rawStdoutDisclosed=false
  result=PASS

  $ node --import tsx /tmp/verify-codex-sandbox-http-streaming-real.mts
  rpcCode=-32603
  message="sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout"
  rawStdoutDisclosed=false
  result=PASS
  node=v26.5.0
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** Both buffered and streaming real WebSocket JSON-RPC paths return internal-error code `-32603` with exactly `sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout`; neither `daemon warning` nor the HTML helper output appears in either message.
- **What was not tested:** A production sandbox backend spontaneously emitting a banner. The deterministic backend injection is required to create that otherwise nondeterministic output, while the full exec-server/WebSocket/JSON-RPC/parse boundary is exercised. The valid-envelope regression is covered by the focused suite.

## Tests and validation

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server.http.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       8 passed (8)

$ ./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/http.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server.http.test.ts
All matched files use the correct format.

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.extensions.json extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/http.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server.http.test.ts
Found 0 warnings and 0 errors.

$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile /tmp/openclaw-98881-extensions.tsbuildinfo
(exit 0)

$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile /tmp/openclaw-98881-extension-tests.tsbuildinfo
(exit 0)

$ node scripts/build-all.mjs
(exit 0)
```

Dependency contract checked directly at OpenAI Codex source commit `7f3eb8a2233aceba3e7962123da84379ee305bb2`: `codex-rs/exec-server-protocol/src/protocol.rs` defines the `http/request` request and `{ status, headers, bodyBase64 }` response envelope; `codex-rs/exec-server/src/client/rpc_http_client.rs` sends it through the shared JSON-RPC client.

## Risk checklist

- User-visible behavior: Yes (intended and bounded): malformed successful helper output now has an attributable sanitized error.
- Config/env/migration behavior: No.
- Security/auth/secrets/network/tool execution: Security improvement only; raw helper stdout is not copied into the error and no execution path changes.
- Plugins/providers/channels/SDK: Codex plugin-internal implementation; no SDK or protocol shape changes.
- Highest-risk area: accidental differences between buffered and streaming malformed-output handling.
- Mitigation: buffered and streaming valid/malformed regressions, exact message/non-disclosure assertions, two real WebSocket JSON-RPC runtime proofs, LOC ratchet, prod/test type gates, lint/format, and full build.

## CI provenance

The preceding exact-head CI failures were inspected from the job logs. The Codex file growth triggered `checks-fast-loc-ratchet`; this revision is back to the current-main 506 physical-line baseline and `check-ts-max-loc` passes. The remaining prior CI failures are upstream-only: `src/agents/model-fallback.test.ts:3764` fails `preserve-caught-error`, and `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/types.ts` reports `BrowserRouteHandler` as unused. Neither file is in this PR diff.

Closes: N/A (no existing issue)


## Latest-main CI refresh

Rebased the original branch onto `upstream/main` `ab95871dd52e035db5e4fd97ebf1d92d8878040a` and force-pushed current exact head `a78496cf4a535d46f62b2131c26870c5f6146663` to trigger a fresh merge-tree CI run. This supersedes the old `check-dependencies` failure, which was from a previous merge tree and reported an upstream dead export outside the Codex diff.

Focused buffered/streaming runtime proofs, 8 focused tests, format, oxlint, prod/test tsgo, LOC ratchet, and full build all pass after this rebase.

target.title: fix(cron): support current and session: targets in initial delivery resolution
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveInitialCronDelivery` in `src/cron/service/initial-delivery.ts` only checks `sessionTarget === "isolated"` when deciding whether to inject default `{ mode: "announce" }` delivery. All other cron code paths already treat `"isolated"`, `"current"`, and `"session:"` as equivalent for this purpose, creating an inconsistency.

## Why This Change Was Made

After #98947 restored persistent session targets, the three sessionTarget values are treated identically in:
- `delivery-plan.ts:106-114` — `isDetachedOutputJob` check
- `normalize.ts:680-684` — `isDetachedDeliveryJob` check
- `jobs.ts:288-298` — `isIsolatedLike` check

But `initial-delivery.ts` was not updated, so cron jobs created with `--session-target current` or `--session-target session:...` would not get the default announce delivery at creation time.

## User Impact

Users creating cron jobs with `sessionTarget: "current"` or `"session:"` may miss delivery announcements.

## Evidence

**Real behavior proof — reproduced via node:**
```
Input:  sessionTarget="current", payload.kind="agentTurn"
OLD:    undefined  <- missing default announce delivery
NEW:    {mode:"announce"}  <- consistent with delivery-plan, normalize, jobs
```

**Validation:**
- tsgo typecheck: passed
- `pnpm test src/cron/service/`: 152 tests (15 files) passed
